newsitem.title: UK: British "information revolution" a myth -- study.
newsitem.headline: British "information revolution" a myth -- study.

text.p: The much-vaunted information revolution remains a myth in Britain, with new technology affecting people in the workplace but not in the home, according to a study released on Tuesday.

The initial data from futura.com, a three-year study examining the impact of the media, communications and technologies, found that people do not feel left behind by advances in technology and are chossing to wait and see if new technologies offer real benefits.

"Data ... suggests that the British public is unimpressed with the claims made by new technology, and that the information revolution is a myth, with new technology making an impact in the workplace but not in people's homes," futura.com said in a statement.

The study, which is being administered by Ogilvy & Mather and the Institute of Communications Studies at the University of Leeds, surveyed 5,000 individuals. The initial results will be used as a baseline to measure change over the next three years as the study continues.

Futura.com found that 76 percent of the British workforce do not use a personal computer on a regular basis. Of those surveyed, 27 percent have access to a computer at home, but only 18 percent of this group regularly use them.

Asked if they were thinking of getting a computer, 62 percent of respondents said no. The reasons cited included: 64 percent said they could see no need for one; 19 percent said too expensive; 15 percent said they don't understand computers; six percent said they do other things with their time at home, and three percent said they dislike technology.

The study also found sharp differences in perceptions of the usefulness of technology in the home versus how PCs are actually used. Of respondents who said they were thinking of getting a computer, 51 percent said the motivation was for child education, nine percent for Internet access, and three percent for e-mail. But of individuals who already use PCs at home, 61 percent said they are used for games, 59 percent for word processing, and 35 percent for child education.

But the survey found that many technologies are readily accepted, with 99 percent of respondents having televisions, 80 percent owning video recorders, 18 percent with a mobile phone and two percent with a car phone.
The study is being sponsored by the Independent Television Commission, Ford, Guinness, Lever, Flextech, Telewest Communications and the Royal Mail.
